topic: El pájaro Toh (turquoise-browed motmot, Eumomota superciliosa)
summary: Usable, with hedging. A consistent, family-friendly core exists across a Mexican government bulletin (CONANP), an educational site (SEP) and tourism/cultural retellings: the toh was a proud, vain bird who dodged the shared work when a storm was coming, hid and slept with his tail sticking out, and lost his fine tail feathers, leaving only two long bare feathers with small tufts; the other birds laughed and he hid away in shame. No ethnographic or folklorist source and no named village narrator was found; all retellings are popular. The 'clock' link is solid (the swinging tail, pájaro reloj). A 'weather' link and 'guardian of the forest' are NOT supported (the storm is only a plot event). 'Guardian of cenotes/underworld' is a tourism/Wikipedia claim; the CONANP version does not say it. No documented motmot motif in Yucatec Maya art was found. Tell it as 'cuentan que...' (they say), keep to the storm-shelter core, avoid underworld/death.
facts: The toh is the turquoise-browed motmot, Eumomota superciliosa. Spanish names: pájaro reloj ('clock bird'), momoto cejiazul. Range: Yucatán Peninsula south to Costa Rica. (Wikipedia; Yucatan Today; Landuum; TV Azteca)

Name: the 19th-century naturalist Boucard (Proc. Zool. Soc. London, 1883, species no. 119) wrote that the bird's cry is 'Toh', said with broad emphasis, hence its Maya name, and that in Maya the word means 'straight', referring to the two long straight tail feathers. Single source; not confirmed in a modern dictionary in this research.
'Clock': the bird perches and swings its tail from side to side like a clock pendulum, which is why Yucatán calls it pájaro reloj. (Yucatan Today; Wikipedia; Landuum; Royal Resorts; Na'atik)

Tail: two long central feathers with bare shafts ending in racket-shaped tips. In real life the barbs wear off through abrasion and preening; the bird does not pluck them (Wikipedia, citing Murphy 2007). The legend explains the tail differently.

Where it lives: digs burrow nests in earth banks and soft limestone, cenote walls, caves, water wells and quarries, and in Maya ruins (Uxmal, Chichén Itzá). Boucard (1883): common in towns wherever there are wells or cenotes; never leaves its well home even though people draw water daily; he once saw about 100 leave one cenote. (Boucard; Yucatan Today; Royal Resorts; TV Azteca; Conrad)
Food: mostly insects (beetles, ants, dragonflies, caterpillars), also small lizards and sometimes small snakes or frogs; it waits on a branch and darts out to catch prey. (Yucatan Today; TV Azteca)
Seen in towns on wires and branches as well as at cenotes and ruins; Yucatan Today says it is widely known in Yucatán by its Maya name toh.

CONANP (Mexican government protected-areas commission) version, credited to its Boletín de Aves en Áreas Naturales Protegidas 27, author Juan Carlos Cuevas Galeana: Toh is proud, thinks his tail and 'royal' status excuse him from work and makes others fetch his food. A storm approaches the peninsula; Kukul (the quetzal, king of the birds) calls all birds to build a shelter (cutting branches, carrying limbs, gathering grass). Toh refuses, then after much pleading agrees, soon tires and hides in the cracks of a cenote and falls asleep with his tail hanging out. The storm ruins the tail; when he flies to the others they laugh, and he sees two long bare sticks hanging from his tail. Ashamed, he flies to the most hidden part of the forest and digs a hole to hide in; the legend says he still lives there, hidden in the depths of cenotes.

Storm-shelter version in Yucatan Today, Royal Resorts, Sunset Resorts and Wikipedia: proud/lazy 'aristocrat' toh pretends to help or refuses to help before a storm, sleeps tucked in rocks/a crevice with the tail outside, the storm strips the tail to two bare feathers, the others laugh, he is ashamed.

Shared core across versions: (1) the toh is proud/vain or lazy and does not do the shared work; (2) his long tail is lost or damaged while he sleeps; (3) it ends up as two long bare feathers with small tufts at the ends; (4) the other birds laugh; (5) he is ashamed and keeps out of sight.

Race/dawn version (Na'atik Language and Culture Institute): after creation, God holds a race to name the animals; the lazy, beautiful motmot sleeps mid-route, the other animals trample his tail, he reaches the finish crying with two thin tufted feathers; as a permanent 'punishment' he must wake the animals every sunrise, and his tail works like clock hands so he is never late again. This is the only source linking the bird to dawn or time-keeping inside the story.

Fire/seed version (SEP educational site 'Leyendas y lectura', Por Esto 2025, mitosyleyendascr.com 2013): Chaac burns the fields to renew the land and asks birds to save seeds; the toh races ahead, tires and sleeps, other birds step on his tail leaving one feather (SEP/mitosyleyendascr), so he saves only a tomato seed; his eyes turn from black to green like the tomato; the dziú saves the maize. Por Esto's text does not say the tail changed.

Burrow version (Jim Conrad's Naturalist Newsletter, 3 Nov 2008, attributed to Maya oral tradition): an ancestor fled an enemy into his burrow and forgot to pull in his long tail; the world brushing past rubbed part of it bare.
Moral stated or implied: vanity, laziness and not helping others bring embarrassment (Yucatan Today says arrogance; CONANP implies it).

Maya art and village talk: no sourced evidence found of the toh as a motif in Yucatec Maya art or of village sayings about it. The 'Motmot' marker/structure at Copán (Honduras) is an archaeologists' field name; no source found showing it depicts the bird. Do not claim an art tradition.
variants: Storm shelter (most common; CONANP, Yucatan Today, Royal Resorts, Sunset Resorts, Wikipedia): toh avoids helping before a storm, sleeps with tail outside, tail ruined, birds laugh.

Where he hides differs: cenote cracks then deep forest hole (CONANP); rocks/crevice then underworld (Yucatan Today, Sunset); crevice then leaves the forest (Wikipedia); wall crack then hides in forest (Royal Resorts).
Race to be named by God; toh sleeps, tail trampled, must wake animals at dawn (Na'atik).
Fire and seeds with Chaac and the dziú bird; toh tired, tail trampled to one feather, saves tomato seed, eyes turn green (SEP, mitosyleyendascr); Por Esto omits the tail change.
Burrow story: tail rubbed bare when an ancestor forgot to pull it into his burrow (Conrad).
Characters differ: CONANP names Kukul (quetzal king); Royal Resorts names Oc (king vulture) and other birds with Maya names that could not be verified; Wikipedia version has no named helpers.

maya_terms.meaning: the motmot (turquoise-browed motmot, pájaro reloj). Boucard 1883 also records it as 'straight' (the two straight tail feathers). Spelling 'toh' is used by every source; have a speaker confirm standard orthography/tone.
bird (general word) - Retana-Guiascón et al., Huitzil 2023, Yucatec Maya of Campeche
tail - same Huitzil 2023 table (Yucatec Maya, Campeche)

maya_terms.term: ts'ono'ot (Spanish: cenote; also seen as ts'onot, dzonot)
maya_terms.meaning: natural sinkhole with water, 'cenote'; the toh nests in and near them
rain god; appears only in the fire/seed version, not needed for the storm version
the quetzal, king of the birds in the CONANP version
Spanish 'clock bird', everyday name in Yucatán

cautions: No ethnographic or folklorist source and no named village storyteller found. Every retelling is popular (government bulletin, school site, tourism blogs). Present it as 'they say / cuentan' and as one story among versions, not as a documented sacred belief.

Topic framing: 'clock' is supported (pendulum tail, pájaro reloj). 'Weather' is NOT: the storm is only a plot event, and no source says the toh predicts weather. 'Guardian of the forest' was not found. 'Guardian of cenotes' appears in a tourism article title and Sunset Resorts; Wikipedia says 'guardian of the underworld' and cites the CONANP article, but the CONANP text as read does not say that. Do not state any of these as fact.

Avoid death/religion: several versions (Yucatan Today, Sunset Resorts) send the toh 'to the underworld', and the cenote-as-portal-to-underworld idea is religious. Use CONANP's wording instead: he hides in a cenote or a hole in the forest.
CONANP's own closing note says people should not attribute magical traits to animals or treat them as omens; keep the story as a tale, not as a bird that foretells things.
Do not mix versions in one story (storm + race + fire). Pick the storm-shelter core, which the most sources agree on.

Do not use the Royal Resorts character names (Oc, Chujut, Panchel, Mox, Xtut, Baax, Cutz); their Maya spellings and meanings could not be verified. The dziú bird in the fire version also could not be verified, so avoid it.

Meaning 'straight' for toh comes from one 1883 source (Boucard) and was not confirmed in a modern Yucatec dictionary here; hedge it ('some say') or leave it out. Landuum notes another motmot (Momotus momota) is also called toh.
Bird call: Boucard says 'Toh'; Yucatan Today says 'hoop-hoop' or 'mot-mot'. Do not state the call.
Do not say real motmots lose their tails in storms: the real racket forms when barbs wear off through preening. Frame the tail loss as the story's explanation.

Soft ending: the laughing and shame are in every version; keep the mocking gentle and end with the toh living quietly, hidden in cenotes and holes (CONANP). Real toh are easy to see on wires, so say 'shy' rather than 'never seen again'.
Maya art and village talk: nothing sourced found; do not invent. The Copán 'Motmot' name is a field nickname only.

Maya spellings: sources use varied orthographies (Chaac/Chaak/Chac; ts'ono'ot/dzonot). The nej/koj/xiik'/ich terms come from a Campeche Yucatec study (Huitzil 2023); ask a Yucatec speaker to check spelling and glottal marks before publishing.
Could not open the Martin and Martin 1980 Condor note (nesting at Uxmal, Kabah, Sayil) or the Murphy 2007 paper directly; the tail-barb fact rests on Wikipedia.
